section_summary: This section combines a legal analysis rejecting claims that the President could use the Nine-Power Treaty and sections 238 and 245 of Title 22 to embargo shipments to Japan with correspondence about neutrality legislation, scrap iron, oil, molybdenite, and other war materials. State Department officials repeatedly explain that existing law generally does not authorize a Japan-specific embargo and that new legislation would be necessary. The section also documents mounting public and organizational pressure to stop American economic assistance to Japan, including petitions, missionary correspondence, and extensive fundraising and publicity material from the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression.

subfiles.title: Authority of the President to Embargo Goods Destined to Japan (continued)
subfiles.about: The memorandum analyzes whether the President could invoke the Nine-Power Treaty and sections 238 and 245 of Title 22 to stop exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer rejects the contention that private American exports to Japan themselves violate the treaty obligation to respect China's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Because the seizure provisions are penal and require an independently established violation of law, they must be strictly construed and cannot support an embargo on this theory, although the Executive could request voluntary restraint from exporters.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with Congressman John Z. Anderson
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Hamilton records a discussion with Congressman Anderson about exports to Japan, neutrality legislation, sanctions, and treaty observance.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton cautioned that stopping scrap-iron exports alone might not quickly end Japan's war and referred Anderson to hearings and Elizabeth Schumpeter's analysis of sanctions. They also discussed cash-and-carry legislation, the absence of restrictions on raw-material exports, possible import or export embargoes, and aid to China, with Hamilton emphasizing that the Department had not adopted definitive positions.

subfiles.title: Statement on Legal Restrictions Affecting Exports to China and Japan
subfiles.to: Congressman John Z. Anderson and other recipients
subfiles.about: The statement summarizes the limits of existing statutes governing arms and raw-material exports to belligerents.
subfiles.summary: It states that no existing statute authorized restrictions on ordinary manufactured goods or raw materials such as scrap iron. The 1937 Neutrality Act could embargo enumerated arms only after a presidential finding of war, and any such embargo would have to apply equally to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Confidential Transmittal of Anderson Conversation to Peiping
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Peiping embassy a confidential copy of the October 10 Anderson conversation memorandum.
subfiles.summary: The transmittal characterizes the enclosure as a discussion of various aspects of United States relations with Japan. Field distribution also included Tokyo and Chungking.

subfiles.title: Confidential Transmittal of Anderson Conversation to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Tokyo embassy a confidential copy of the October 10 Anderson conversation memorandum.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed memorandum concerned Congressman Anderson's discussion with Hamilton about relations with Japan. The document records parallel field distribution to Tokyo, Peiping, and Chungking.

subfiles.title: Senator Brown's Transmittal of the Williams Letter
subfiles.about: The Senate Committee on Finance cover page transmitted George Way Williams's October 12 letter to the Department of State.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page consists chiefly of Senate letterhead and receipt markings, with the substantive text poorly captured by OCR. The Department's later reply establishes that Brown forwarded Williams's letter for comment.

subfiles.title: Letter from George Way Williams to Senator Brown
subfiles.about: Williams asks whether pending legislation would stop American war-material shipments that sustain Japan's aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: Williams argues that national debate over repeal of the arms embargo risks obscuring the more important conflict in East Asia. He portrays the United States as an arsenal for treaty-breaking Japan and favors action ending material assistance to a war of aggression against friendly China.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Brown Regarding the Williams Letter
subfiles.about: Hull supplies the Department's standard statement and reports the status of bills restricting exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses two copies of a departmental statement for Brown and Williams. He notes that several bills covering arms, scrap iron, oil, and other useful war materials had been introduced but that Congress adjourned without acting on them.

subfiles.title: Letter from Fred H. Lysons to Senator Thomas
subfiles.about: Lysons supports treaty-based restrictions on exports to Japan and argues that the President could stop shipments under section 238 of Title 22.
subfiles.summary: Lysons identifies scrap iron, Pennsylvania high-octane gasoline, and molybdenite as materials Japan could not readily replace and contends that denying them would seriously impede the war. He reasons that knowingly permitting such exports violates the Nine-Power Treaty and makes them seizable as exports made in violation of law.

subfiles.title: Departmental Reply to Senator Thomas on Lysons's Argument
subfiles.about: The Department rejects Lysons's claim that exports to Japan violate the Nine-Power Treaty and can be stopped under section 238.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that lawful private sales and shipments do not bring the government's treaty obligation to respect Chinese sovereignty into question merely because Japan may use the goods in hostilities. Section 238 therefore has no application, and Lysons's letter is returned as requested.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck Comment on Draft Reply to Senator Thomas
subfiles.about: Hornbeck proposes revised language for the Department's response concerning lawful private exports and the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck approves the letter in principle but recommends refining its central sentence. His wording makes clear that the treaty obligation is not implicated by sales and shipments to Japan that American nationals are not otherwise prohibited from making.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser's Proposed Revision of the Thomas Letter
subfiles.about: A handwritten note proposes deleting and rewriting portions of the response to Senator Thomas.
subfiles.summary: The proposed language says that lawful sales and shipments to Japan do not violate the government's treaty obligation merely because officials know or suspect that Japan may use the goods against China. It concludes that section 238 of Title 22 is inapplicable.

subfiles.title: Controls Division Note on Precedent for the Thomas Letter
subfiles.from: J. S. Littell, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Littell notes that the draft repeats language previously used in a letter to Senator Schwellenbach.
subfiles.summary: The brief memorandum identifies the August 22 Schwellenbach reply as the drafting precedent. It documents internal coordination over maintaining a consistent departmental legal position.

subfiles.title: Draft Reply to Senator Thomas on the Lysons Letter
subfiles.about: This earlier draft offers a fuller legal explanation of why section 238 cannot be applied to exports destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The draft emphasizes the government's commitment to scrupulous treaty observance but explains that penal seizure and condemnation statutes require strict construction. Because the Nine-Power Treaty contains no specific prohibition of private shipments, Lysons's proposed use of section 238 is rejected.

subfiles.title: Letter from W. Reginald Wheeler on American Public Opinion
subfiles.about: Wheeler reports widespread American opposition to trade that supports Japan's war against China.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on speaking tours from the Atlantic to the Pacific, Wheeler says audiences objected on moral, commercial, and national-security grounds to shipments and imports involving Japan. He cites polling, support for terminating the commercial treaty, Ambassador Grew's remarks, and a nearly unanimous missionary-conference vote favoring voluntary cessation of war-supply shipments.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to W. Reginald Wheeler
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Wheeler's report on public attitudes toward the Far Eastern conflict.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton states that Wheeler's views and observations have been carefully noted. He expresses appreciation for thoughtful public comment on American foreign relations.

subfiles.title: Bureau of Mines Referral of the Steinmetz Petition
subfiles.about: The Bureau of Mines informs Steinmetz that his group's protest against shipments to Japan has been referred to the Department of State.
subfiles.summary: The Bureau recognizes that the petition opposes scrap iron and other war-material exports. Because the protest concerns foreign policy, the matter is forwarded to the State Department for consideration.

subfiles.title: Seattle Citizens' Protest Against Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: E. M. Steinmetz and other Seattle residents
subfiles.about: Seattle petitioners protest the shipment of scrap iron and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The signatories express concern about large exports through Seattle and other American ports. They describe the trade as support for Japan's violation of the Nine-Power Treaty and American participation in China's suffering and threatened destruction.

subfiles.title: Interior Department Transmittal of the China Club Letter
subfiles.from: Ebert K. Burlew, Acting Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: Burlew forwards the China Club of Seattle's letter and a copy of Interior's reply because the closing argument concerns foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: The two pages preserve the original and signed-copy versions of the same referral. The attachments placed W. E. Priestley's export protest before the State Department for consideration.

subfiles.title: Interior Department Reply to W. E. Priestley
subfiles.from: Ebert K. Burlew, Acting Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: Interior explains its scrap survey and refers Priestley's foreign-policy comments to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Burlew says the September survey was intended to establish reliable data on strategic domestic scrap stocks and was supported by military and industry bodies. Because Priestley's objections to commerce with Japan concerned foreign policy, his letter was sent to State.

subfiles.title: China Club of Seattle Letter on Scrap Iron and Molybdenite
subfiles.from: W. E. Priestley, China Club of Seattle
subfiles.about: Priestley links Seattle exports of scrap iron and molybdenite to Japan's military power and urges support for Schwellenbach's bill.
subfiles.summary: The letter cites 23,000 tons of scrap iron and unusually valuable molybdenite shipments through Seattle, describing both as essential to Japanese armament production. Priestley calls American trade partnership in China's destruction and contrasts it with costly Pacific fortifications against Japan.

subfiles.title: The Guilt of America
subfiles.about: Priestley argues that American materials enable Japan's destruction of China and threaten future United States security.
subfiles.summary: The article describes mass casualties, displacement, bombing, and Japan's goal of subjugating China while asserting that sixty percent of Japanese war materials came from the United States. It warns that a victorious Japan could use China's resources and American-supplied weapons to challenge the United States and ends by demanding a halt to war-material shipments.

subfiles.title: State Department Reply to W. E. Priestley
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that existing law does not authorize the export prohibitions sought by Priestley.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the 1939 Neutrality Act does not prohibit arms exports to belligerents and that, aside from tin-plate scrap and helium, no law permits bans on ordinary products or raw materials such as scrap iron. He adds that Congress had not acted on the several bills introduced to restrict war-material exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter from Egbert W. Smith on the Expiring Japanese Treaty
subfiles.about: Smith asks for assurance that termination of the commercial treaty will end American military supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Smith welcomes the decision to end the treaty on January 26, 1940. Alarmed by reports that a new arrangement might still allow Japan to obtain war supplies, he asks Hull to dispel the concern that American complicity in the conquest of China will continue.

subfiles.title: State Department Reply to Egbert W. Smith
subfiles.about: The Department thanks Smith for endorsing treaty termination but explains that export bans still require legislation.
subfiles.summary: The reply repeats that the 1939 Neutrality Act does not authorize the desired prohibition and that existing law covers only exceptional commodities such as tin-plate scrap and helium. It notes that several Japan-focused export bills had been introduced but not enacted.

subfiles.title: Inquiry Concerning Foreign and Anonymous Contributions
subfiles.about: Price requests a legal ruling on whether the American Committee may accept contributions from Chinese nationals or anonymous sources.
subfiles.summary: Price describes the Committee's American control and financing, then presents cases involving gifts passed through Mr. Lowe from Mr. Shoong and Mr. Foong, a visiting Chinese donor, and anonymous contributions. He asks whether the organization must investigate citizenship and the ultimate source of every gift and encloses examples of its fundraising literature and program statement.

subfiles.title: Fundraising Appeal Following Termination of the Commercial Treaty
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The Committee solicits funds for the next phase of its campaign to stop American war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The circular claims popular pressure helped persuade the administration to terminate the commercial treaty and outlines publicity, lobbying, and organizational work before the next congressional session. It supplies expenditure and contribution totals, notes staff reductions, and urges donors to finance renewed campaigning.

subfiles.title: Stop Arming Japan: Chungking Bombing Appeal
subfiles.from: Mrs. Sidney D. Gamble, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The leaflet reproduces an eyewitness cable about the bombing of Chungking and requests immediate campaign contributions.
subfiles.summary: The cable describes destroyed civilian districts and hospitals, heavy casualties, fires, and approximately one hundred thousand homeless people while reporting that Chinese morale remained intact. The Committee uses the account to demand intensified opposition to American aid for Japan and funding for speakers, radio, press, research, and Washington representation.

subfiles.title: Stimson Acts to Curb War Sales to Japan
subfiles.about: The article announces formation of the American Committee and its campaign for legislation restricting American supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The clipping presents Henry L. Stimson and other prominent sponsors as supporting public education, voluntary commercial restraint, executive action, and legislation against economic assistance for Japanese aggression. It reproduces the Committee's rationale and lists numerous sponsoring figures and their affiliations.

subfiles.title: Philadelphia Appeal Supporting the American Committee
subfiles.about: The signatory endorses the Committee's educational campaign and asks Philadelphians to support it financially.
subfiles.summary: The letter invokes Walter Judd's characterization of America as Japan's armorer and says the movement to stop sales to the Japanese military has expanded nationwide. It praises the Committee's informative, non-hysterical approach and directs support to executive director Harry Price.

subfiles.title: Nationwide Campaign Appeal to Stop War Supplies for Japan
subfiles.about: Greene seeks at least $50,000 for a nationwide campaign against American material support of Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The circular argues that scrap iron, oil, steel, trucks, and machinery are more important to Japan than finished munitions and condemns the contradiction between supplying Japan and arming against aggressor states. It proposes using newspapers, magazines, pamphlets, radio, and speakers to generate demand for legislation stopping war supplies.

subfiles.title: Stop Arming Japan: Duplicate Chungking Cable Appeal
subfiles.from: Elizabeth Lowe Gamble, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: A duplicate version of the Chungking bombing leaflet asks readers to finance the campaign against American aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reproduced eyewitness cable emphasizes civilian devastation, destroyed hospitals, homelessness, and the absence of important military results from the bombing. The surrounding appeal calls for funds to sustain speakers, publications, radio work, research, and legislative advocacy.

subfiles.title: American Scrap Iron and American Wheels in China
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The illustrated leaflet traces American metal, gasoline, vehicles, and machinery into Japanese military operations in China.
subfiles.summary: “The Saga of American Scrap Iron in China” depicts scrap and gasoline becoming bombs and shrapnel used against Chinese civilians. “The Japanese Juggernaut Rolls Across China on American Wheels” attributes Japanese mobility to American trucks, motors, armored cars, motorcycles, buses, and automobiles and asks readers to help stop the traffic.

subfiles.title: A Brief Report on Progress
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The Committee reports on its publicity, organizing, lobbying, publications, speakers, finances, and future plans.
subfiles.summary: The report claims a nationwide movement involving thousands of individuals, more than thirty local committees in twenty states, extensive publications, public communications to government, and international contacts. It names Walter H. Judd, George Fitch, and Freda Utley as major speakers and states that further expansion depends on new contributions.

subfiles.title: America Supports Japanese Aggression
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: The brochure lists the Committee's sponsors and board and argues that American exports strengthen Japan at the expense of China and American security.
subfiles.summary: The text contends that the United States supplied more than half of Japan's essential war-material imports in 1937 and 1938 and was helping create a potentially dominant military empire. It argues that withholding support from Japan while aiding China's economic survival would improve Pacific security, conserve strategic resources, protect long-term trade, and answer Americans' moral revulsion at aggression.
